_meta: Three token embeddings and a per-position vector, used to show that self-attention with no positional information is permutation-equivariant -- reorder the input tokens and the output vectors are the same, merely reordered the same way -- so the model literally cannot tell one word order from another, which is exactly why positional encodings exist. Self-attention computes each token's output as a softmax-weighted average of all tokens' values, and the weights come from dot products between tokens; nothing in that computation refers to a token's position, only to which tokens are present. So if you permute the input rows by some permutation pi, the output rows come out permuted by the same pi and are otherwise identical: attn(permute(X)) == permute(attn(X)). A consequence is that any order-blind readout -- mean pooling over the outputs, for instance -- gives the identical vector for 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog', because the two are permutations of each other and pooling erases the order the permutation carried. The fix is to add positional information: a per-position vector p_i is added to the token at position i, so position 0 always contributes p_0 no matter which token sits there. Now permuting the tokens does NOT permute the augmented input -- the token that moves to position 0 picks up p_0, not the p it had before -- so the outputs genuinely differ and the two word orders become distinguishable. The tokens are orthonormal one-hot embeddings (dog, bites, man), the permutation reverses the sequence to (man, bites, dog), and the position vectors are fixed; every attention output, the pooled representations, and the equivariance checks are computed. Stdlib only.
